title: Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 11: the vision of the universal form
excerpt: Arjuna sees the world within Krishna: divine splendour, the destruction of warriors and time itself, before returning to a gentler encounter.
introHtml:
Arjuna asks to see Krishna’s universal form and receives the divine eye needed to behold it. He sees gods, worlds and warriors entering its devouring mouths. Krishna declares himself Time, destroyer of worlds, and tells Arjuna to rise and kill the warriors already slain by him. Arjuna praises Krishna, asks forgiveness and requests a gentler form. The chapter concludes with the requirement of undivided devotion.

Each Meaning renders the Sanskrit in English. Each Explanation follows the verse’s statements, terms and argument. Named traditional interpretations are distinguished where they differ. [1–2]

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Through the supreme, inward teaching that you have spoken out of kindness toward me, this delusion of mine has gone.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that the supreme secret teaching about the self has removed his delusion. He attributes the instruction to Krishna's kindness toward him. Adhyātma names its subject as the self and its deepest reality. This acknowledgement introduces his request to see the divine form: the one whose teaching has dispelled his confusion is now asked to disclose his sovereign appearance.

verses.meaningHtml: For I have heard from you in detail about the arising and passing away of beings, lotus-eyed one, and also about your imperishable greatness.
verses.explanationHtml: The two subjects belong together: beings arise and disappear, while the divine greatness on which they depend is described as imperishable. Chapters 7–10 have explained that relationship through nature, cosmic cycles and particular manifestations. Arjuna recalls that preparation rather than asking for an unrelated spectacle. The affectionate address “lotus-eyed” also preserves the personal relationship from which his request for a universal vision emerges.

verses.meaningHtml: Supreme Lord, it is as you have declared yourself to be. Yet I wish to see your sovereign form, highest Person.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna affirms that Krishna is as he has declared himself to be, then asks to see his sovereign form. Aiśvara describes divine lordship and its power. Arjuna has heard of Krishna's sourcehood, pervasion and manifestations; he now wants that greatness made visible. He addresses him as the highest Person while requesting the form in which his sovereignty can be seen.

verses.meaningHtml: If you think that I am able to see it, Lord, then, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks Krishna to show his imperishable self if Krishna considers him able to see it. The decision is left with the Lord, addressed as the master of yoga. The request links Arjuna's capacity to receive the vision with Krishna's judgement and power. Krishna will answer by granting a divine eye through which the form can be seen.

verses.meaningHtml: The blessed Lord said: Look, Partha, at my forms in their hundreds and thousands, divine and varied in colour and shape.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna commands Arjuna to look at his divine forms in their hundreds and thousands. They differ in colour and shape. The reply to the request for his sovereign form begins with this multitude, which the following verses fill with named divine hosts and the entire world. Arjuna is to behold these many forms through the sight Krishna grants.

verses.meaningHtml: See the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Ashvins and the Maruts. See many wonders never seen before, descendant of Bharata.
verses.explanationHtml: These are named groups within the inherited divine world, several already encountered among Chapter 10's manifestations. The Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, twin Ashvins and Maruts are now to be seen together. “Never seen before” makes the disclosure new for Arjuna even though the divine names are familiar. The vision gathers known sacred categories into an unprecedented whole, preparing for its further inclusion of earthly beings and the battlefield.

verses.meaningHtml: See here today, within my body and gathered in one place, the entire world with all that moves and does not move, and whatever else you wish to see, Gudakesha.
verses.explanationHtml: The promise is comprehensive. Moving and unmoving encompass living creatures and the apparently fixed world; neither lies outside the divine body disclosed here. Gathering everything “in one place” overturns the ordinary experience of separated locations and successive observations. The reference to whatever else Arjuna wishes to see leaves room for the personal question that will soon dominate him: what this universal reality means for the warriors standing before him.

verses.meaningHtml: But you cannot see me with this eye of your own. I give you a divine eye: behold my sovereign yoga.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that Arjuna's own eye cannot see him in this form. He therefore gives Arjuna a divine eye and commands him to behold his sovereign yoga. Both the form and the capacity to see it come from Krishna. The disclosure that follows is made possible by this grant of divine sight.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Having spoken in this way, king, Hari, the great master of yoga, then showed Partha his supreme sovereign form.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya addresses Dhritarashtra, the king to whom he narrates the battlefield dialogue. He reports that Hari, Krishna, has shown Arjuna the supreme sovereign form. The description as the great master of yoga identifies the power by which Krishna discloses it. The preceding promise of divine sight is now followed by the revelation itself, whose features Sanjaya describes in the next verses.

verses.meaningHtml: It had many mouths and eyes, many astonishing sights, many divine ornaments, and many divine weapons raised.
verses.explanationHtml: The first description accumulates details rather than defining an outline. Mouths and eyes multiply, while ornaments and raised weapons combine splendour with power. The weapons are present from the beginning, anticipating the terrible aspect that later overwhelms Arjuna. At this stage Sanjaya's emphasis remains on wonder: the form draws together the signs of divine majesty in numbers that defeat the usual expectation of a single body's shape.

verses.meaningHtml: It wore divine garlands and garments, was anointed with divine perfumes, and was wholly wondrous, radiant, infinite and facing in every direction.
verses.explanationHtml: Garlands, clothing and fragrance extend the description beyond anatomy and weaponry into the ceremonial language of divine presence. Facing every direction means that the form cannot be confined to the side from which an observer approaches it. “Infinite” similarly prevents the accumulated features from becoming a bounded portrait. The sensory richness offers ways to imagine the disclosure, while the final terms continually exceed any ordinary image assembled from them.

verses.meaningHtml: If the radiance of a thousand suns were to rise together in the sky, it might resemble the splendour of that great being.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya compares the splendour of the great form to a thousand suns rising simultaneously in the sky. The comparison conveys the immense radiance of the vision, and its conditional wording presents even that brightness as a possible likeness. It follows the description of divine ornaments, garlands and weapons and precedes Arjuna's sight of the whole world gathered within the divine body.

verses.meaningHtml: There, in the body of the God of gods, Pandava then saw the entire world, divided in many ways, gathered together in one place.
verses.explanationHtml: The promise of verse 11.7 is now fulfilled. Diversity remains visible: the world is still “divided in many ways,” even while held within one body. The vision therefore includes both multiplicity and an encompassing unity. Calling Krishna the God of gods locates even the divine hosts within that whole. Arjuna's seeing now reaches beyond the selected examples of Chapter 10 to the world they had indicated.

verses.meaningHtml: Then Dhananjaya, filled with wonder and with the hairs of his body standing up, bowed his head to the god and spoke with his hands joined.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna is filled with wonder, his hair stands on end, and he bows his head with his hands joined. Dhananjaya is another name for him. Sanjaya describes these bodily signs of astonishment and reverence before giving Arjuna's own words. Arjuna then names the gods, sages and beings he sees within the form and declares that he can find none of its limits.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Within your body, God, I see all the gods and the various hosts of beings, the lord Brahma seated upon the lotus, all the sages and the divine serpents.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna begins naming what he sees, locating the divine world and its beings within Krishna. Brahma's lotus seat, the sages and the celestial serpents give specific content to Sanjaya's earlier account of multiplicity. The list is not confined to human life or the battlefield. Its breadth makes the later appearance of individual warriors more startling: those familiar persons will be encountered within the same all-encompassing form.

verses.meaningHtml: I see you with countless arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, infinite in form on every side. I see neither your end, nor your middle, nor your beginning, Lord of the universe, universal form.
verses.explanationHtml: The language of many bodily parts meets a failure to locate any boundary or centre. Arjuna can describe features, but he cannot establish a beginning, middle or end that would make the form manageable as an ordinary object. “Universal form,” viśvarūpa, names this comprehensive disclosure. His repeated “I see” conveys immediacy, while his inability to find limits shows how radically the sight exceeds the conditions of familiar seeing.

verses.meaningHtml: I see you crowned, bearing a mace and a discus, a mass of radiance shining everywhere, difficult to look upon, blazing all around like fire and the sun, immeasurable.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna sees a crown, mace and discus within the immeasurable form. Its radiance shines on every side, like the brightness of fire and the sun, making it difficult to behold. The familiar divine attributes are joined to overwhelming brilliance. The statement continues his account of the form whose beginning, middle and end he has been unable to find.

verses.meaningHtml: You are the imperishable, the supreme reality to be known. You are the highest resting place of this universe. You are the unfailing guardian of eternal dharma. I understand you to be the eternal Person.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna identifies Krishna as the imperishable, the highest reality to be known and the supreme resting place of the universe. He also calls him the guardian of eternal dharma and the eternal Person. These declarations apply the names of ultimate reality to the form before him. Arjuna states this as his understanding of the one he now sees.

verses.meaningHtml: I see you without beginning, middle or end, of infinite power and with innumerable arms, with the moon and sun as your eyes, your face a blazing fire, heating this universe with your radiance.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna sees a form with neither beginning, middle nor end, possessed of infinite power and innumerable arms. The sun and moon are its eyes, and its face blazes like fire. Its radiance heats the whole universe. These cosmic features continue the account of the immeasurable form, while the burning face and heat lead into the terror and destruction described next.

verses.meaningHtml: For the space between heaven and earth, and every direction, is filled by you alone. Seeing this wondrous and terrible form of yours, great self, the three worlds tremble.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna alone fills the space between heaven and earth and every direction. The three worlds tremble on seeing his extraordinary and terrible form. Arjuna describes the extent of the form and the fear it produces throughout the cosmos. The divine hosts named next enter it or stand praising it in fear and astonishment.

verses.meaningHtml: These hosts of gods are entering you. Some, afraid, praise you with joined hands. Hosts of great sages and perfected beings cry “May there be well-being!” and praise you with abundant hymns.
verses.explanationHtml: Different beings respond through entrance, fear, prayer and praise. The cry svasti invokes well-being, giving the cosmic scene a ceremonial voice even as anxiety spreads through it. Perfected beings, siddhas, stand alongside the great sages rather than ordinary human observers alone. Their reactions show that Arjuna's difficulty is part of the vision's wider effect: the divine hosts themselves meet the universal form with a mixture of reverence and apprehension.

verses.meaningHtml: The Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, the two Ashvins, Maruts and heat-drinking ancestors, and hosts of Gandharvas, Yakshas, Asuras and perfected beings all gaze at you in astonishment.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna lists the divine and celestial hosts gazing at Krishna in astonishment. They include the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Ashvins and Maruts, together with Gandharvas, Yakshas, Asuras and perfected beings. Uṣmapāḥ, “heat-drinkers,” names the ancestors who receive offerings. All these groups stand within the scene and witness the universal form.

verses.meaningHtml: Seeing your vast form, mighty-armed one, with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs and feet, many bellies and terrible fangs, the worlds tremble, and so do I.
verses.explanationHtml: The vast form has many mouths, eyes, arms, thighs, feet and bellies, together with terrible fangs. Arjuna says that the worlds tremble at its sight and that he too trembles. The fangs add the destructive feature that will dominate the following descriptions. His own fear is stated alongside the fear of the worlds.

verses.meaningHtml: Seeing you touching the sky, blazing with many colours, with gaping mouths and enormous shining eyes, my inner self is shaken. I find neither steadiness nor peace, Vishnu.
verses.explanationHtml: The form reaches the sky, blazes in many colours and has enormous shining eyes and open mouths. Arjuna says that the sight shakes his inner being and deprives him of steadiness and peace. He addresses Krishna as Vishnu. The account joins the visible features of the form to Arjuna's declared fear and loss of composure.

verses.meaningHtml: Seeing your mouths with terrible fangs, like the fires at the end of time, I no longer know the directions and find no refuge. Be gracious, Lord of gods, dwelling place of the universe.
verses.explanationHtml: The fanged mouths appear like the fires that destroy the world at the end of time. Arjuna loses his sense of direction and finds no comfort or refuge. He asks for grace from the very Lord whose form terrifies him, calling him the Lord of gods and dwelling place of the universe. The appeal follows directly from the sight of those consuming mouths.

verses.meaningHtml: All these sons of Dhritarashtra, together with the hosts of kings, Bhishma, Drona and the charioteer's son Karna, along with the chief warriors on our own side—
verses.explanationHtml: The cosmic scene becomes the immediate battlefield. Arjuna names opponents bound to him by kinship, honour and instruction, including Bhishma and his teacher Drona. The charioteer's son identifies Karna, while “our own side” makes clear that destruction is not limited to the enemy. The sentence runs directly into the next verse. These are the people whose deaths haunted Arjuna in Chapter 1, now seen within the universal form itself.

verses.meaningHtml: They rush into your frightening mouths, terrible with fangs. Some are seen caught between your teeth, their heads crushed to pieces.
verses.explanationHtml: The warriors named in 11.26 rush into Krishna's fanged mouths. Some are caught between the teeth with their heads crushed to pieces. The vision shows the deaths of Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Dhritarashtra's sons and warriors on Arjuna's own side. These identifiable persons enter the destructive divine form that Arjuna has been describing.

verses.meaningHtml: As the many currents of rivers rush toward the ocean alone, so these heroes of the human world enter your blazing mouths.
verses.explanationHtml: The movement of the warriors into Krishna's mouths is compared to rivers rushing into the ocean. Many streams converge upon one destination, just as the heroes of the human world enter the blazing mouths. The comparison describes the force and direction of their entry. The following verse adds the image of moths entering a fire toward destruction.

verses.meaningHtml: As moths hurry into a blazing flame toward their destruction, so these people hurry into your mouths toward their destruction.
verses.explanationHtml: Moths rush into a burning flame and perish in it. Arjuna sees the same haste toward destruction in the people entering Krishna's mouths. Destruction is repeated in the comparison and its application to the warriors. The river image described their convergence; the moth image states the death that awaits those entering the blazing form.

verses.meaningHtml: Devouring all the worlds with blazing mouths, you lick them up on every side. Your fierce radiances fill the entire universe with brilliance and scorch it, Vishnu.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna's blazing mouths devour all the worlds, licking them up on every side. His fierce radiance fills and scorches the universe. Arjuna again addresses him as Vishnu while describing this destruction. The sight moves beyond the warriors entering the mouths to the consumption of all worlds, leading to his question about the terrible form's identity and purpose.

verses.meaningHtml: Tell me who you are in this terrible form. Homage to you, highest God; be gracious. I wish to know you, the primal one, for I do not understand your undertaking.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna's question concerns identity through action: what is this form doing, and toward what end? He has already praised Krishna as the imperishable reality, yet that recognition has not explained the devouring spectacle. Homage and a plea for grace accompany the request, showing that inquiry continues within reverence. The direct admission of not understanding prepares Krishna's famous answer, in which the destructive force is named as time.

verses.meaningHtml: The blessed Lord said: I am Time, grown mighty, destroyer of worlds, engaged here in bringing the worlds to an end. Even without you, all these warriors standing in the opposing ranks will cease to be.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna identifies himself as Kāla, Time, grown mighty and destroying worlds. He says that his present undertaking is their destruction. All the warriors in the opposing ranks will cease to exist even without Arjuna's action. This answers the question about the terrible form's purpose and precedes the command that Arjuna arise and take part in the killing already accomplished by Krishna.

verses.meaningHtml: Therefore arise, win renown, defeat your enemies and enjoy a flourishing kingdom. They have already been slain by me. Be merely the instrument, Savyasachin.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna commands Arjuna to arise, win renown, defeat his enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. He says that he has already slain the opponents and that Arjuna is to be merely his instrument. Savyasachin praises Arjuna's ability to wield the bow with either hand. That skilled warrior is now ordered to accomplish the victory whose victims Krishna declares already killed.

verses.meaningHtml: Strike down Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha, Karna and the other warrior heroes whom I have already slain. Do not tremble. Fight: you will conquer your enemies in battle.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna names Drona, Bhishma, Jayadratha and Karna among the warriors Arjuna must strike down. Drona is his teacher and Bhishma his revered elder. Krishna again says that he has already slain them. He commands Arjuna to overcome his trembling and fight, promising victory over his enemies in battle. The names specify the killing required of him.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Hearing these words of Keshava, the crowned Arjuna trembled, joined his hands and bowed. Overwhelmed with fear, he again bowed and spoke to Krishna in a faltering voice.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna trembles after hearing Krishna's declaration and command. He bows repeatedly with joined hands and answers in a faltering voice, overcome by fear. Sanjaya describes him as crowned, identifying the warrior who receives the order. The visible trembling and broken speech continue Arjuna's response to the destructive form even after Krishna has explained its undertaking.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: It is fitting, Hrishikesha, that the world delights in your praise and grows devoted, that terrified Rakshasas flee in every direction, and that all the hosts of perfected beings bow to you.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that the world's delight and devotion are fitting responses to Krishna's praise. Rakshasas flee from him in terror, while the hosts of perfected beings bow. These responses are presented together as appropriate to his greatness. Hrishikesha, the name used in the address, describes Krishna as Lord of the senses. Arjuna continues by declaring why all beings should bow before him.

verses.meaningHtml: Why should they not bow to you, great self, greater even than Brahma and the first creator? Infinite Lord of gods, dwelling place of the universe, you are the imperishable, being and non-being, and what is beyond them.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna says that Krishna is greater than Brahma and the first creator, so all beings have reason to bow before him. He calls him infinite, Lord of gods and the universe's dwelling place. Krishna is identified as the imperishable, as sat and asat—being and non-being—and as what lies beyond both. The praise asserts his priority to the creator and his transcendence of these paired terms.

verses.meaningHtml: You are the primal God, the ancient Person. You are the highest resting place of this universe. You are the knower and what is to be known, and the supreme abode. By you the universe is pervaded, infinite in form.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna calls Krishna the primal God and ancient Person, the universe's highest resting place and supreme abode. He identifies him as both the knower and what is to be known. The universe is pervaded by his infinite form. These names join origin, knowledge, support and destination in Arjuna's account of the God before whom he bows.

verses.meaningHtml: You are Vayu, Yama, Agni, Varuna, the moon, Prajapati and the great-grandfather. Homage, homage to you a thousand times; again and again, homage to you.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna identifies Krishna with Vayu, Yama, Agni, Varuna, the moon and Prajapati. The great-grandfather places him before the world's progenitors as well. These divine identities are followed by repeated homage, offered a thousand times and again and again. The many names and salutations continue his recognition of the universal form as encompassing the gods and their powers.

verses.meaningHtml: Homage to you in front and behind; homage to you on every side, you who are all. Infinite in strength and immeasurable in might, you pervade everything, and therefore you are everything.
verses.explanationHtml: The directions reappear as occasions for homage. Earlier Arjuna lost his bearings before the terrible mouths; now he bows in every direction because no direction lies beyond the presence he addresses. Pervasion leads him to the declaration “you are everything,” continuing the chapter's language of comprehensive identity. The verse turns the impossibility of finding an outside viewpoint into a form of worship, without yet resolving his fear of the vision.

verses.meaningHtml: Thinking of you as a friend, I rashly said “Krishna,” “Yadava,” “friend,” unaware of this greatness of yours, through carelessness or affection—
verses.explanationHtml: The universal vision changes Arjuna's understanding of his ordinary relationship with Krishna. Names he had used in friendship now seem inadequate to the greatness disclosed. He does not deny that affection motivated him; affection itself is named alongside carelessness as the source of his informality. The unfinished sentence continues into the next verse, where familiar occasions of shared life become the setting for his request for forgiveness.

verses.meaningHtml: And whatever disrespect I showed you in jest, while playing, resting, sitting or eating, whether alone or before others, unfailing one—for all of it I ask your forgiveness, immeasurable one.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks forgiveness for disrespect shown through joking during recreation, rest, sitting and meals. He includes occasions when they were alone and when others were present. The confession continues the preceding account of addressing Krishna simply as friend without knowing his greatness. Calling him unfailing and immeasurable, Arjuna asks pardon for all those acts of familiarity.

verses.meaningHtml: You are the father of the world, of all that moves and does not move. You are its venerable and greatest teacher. None is your equal; how then could any be greater, in the three worlds, you of incomparable power?
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna calls Krishna the father of all moving and unmoving beings and their greatest, most venerable teacher. No one in the three worlds equals him, and no one can therefore be greater. The declaration gives universal scope to his authority and power. It leads into Arjuna's appeal that this supreme father and teacher forgive his former familiarity.

verses.meaningHtml: Therefore I bow down, prostrating my body, and ask your grace, worshipful Lord. As a father bears with a son, a friend with a friend, and a beloved with the beloved, God, you should bear with me.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna prostrates his body and asks Krishna to bear with him. He gives three comparisons for the forgiveness he seeks: a father with a son, a friend with a friend, and a beloved with the beloved. The request concerns the disrespect through familiarity confessed in 11.41–42. Arjuna asks for grace from the Lord whom he has just declared unequalled in all three worlds.

verses.meaningHtml: I am delighted to have seen what was never seen before, yet my mind is shaken by fear. Show me that form of yours, God; be gracious, Lord of gods, dwelling place of the universe.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna declares both delight at the unprecedented vision and fear that shakes his mind. He asks Krishna to show the earlier form and to be gracious. The same Lord is addressed as Lord of gods and dwelling place of the universe. The following verse specifies the appearance Arjuna wants to see: crowned, bearing mace and discus, with four arms.

verses.meaningHtml: I wish to see you just so, crowned, holding the mace and discus. Take that same four-armed form, thousand-armed one, universal form.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna asks Krishna to take the four-armed form bearing crown, mace and discus. He addresses the universal form as thousand-armed while requesting this particular appearance. The many arms of the terrifying disclosure are thus contrasted with the four arms he wishes to see. His request follows the admission that the universal vision has filled him with both delight and fear.

verses.meaningHtml: The blessed Lord said: Out of favour toward you, Arjuna, I have shown you through my own yoga this supreme form, radiant, universal, infinite and primal, which no one other than you has seen before.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that he has shown the supreme form out of favour toward Arjuna and through his own yoga. He names it radiant, universal, infinite and primal. No one other than Arjuna has seen it before. The verse attributes the revelation to Krishna's power and grace and states the exceptional position of its recipient.

verses.meaningHtml: Neither through Vedic study and sacrifice, nor through gifts, rites or severe austerities, can I be seen in this form in the human world by anyone other than you, hero of the Kurus.
verses.explanationHtml: Vedic learning, sacrifice, gifts, rites and severe austerities cannot produce the sight of this form that Arjuna has received. Krishna says that no one else in the human world can see him in this way through those practices. The statement continues his declaration that the vision has been given to Arjuna through favour and his own yoga.

verses.meaningHtml: Do not be distressed or bewildered at seeing this terrible form of mine. Free from fear and with a glad heart, behold again that same form of mine.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna now addresses the distress caused by the revelation. He acknowledges its terrible character and directs Arjuna toward a renewed sight that can restore gladness. The instruction echoes the earlier invitation to behold, but its purpose has changed: seeing will now relieve the fear that seeing awakened. The verse makes reassurance part of the encounter itself, keeping the destructive universal form and the approachable divine presence within the same speaker.

verses.meaningHtml: Sanjaya said: Having spoken so to Arjuna, Vasudeva again showed his own form. Becoming gentle in form once more, the great self comforted the frightened Arjuna.
verses.explanationHtml: Sanjaya reports that Vasudeva shows his own form again and becomes gentle in appearance. He comforts Arjuna, who remains afraid after the universal vision. Vasudeva is Krishna's name. The change fulfils the promise in 11.49 that Arjuna will again behold the earlier form, free from the terror produced by the devouring mouths.

verses.meaningHtml: Arjuna said: Seeing this gentle human form of yours, Janardana, I have now regained my composure and returned to my normal state.
verses.explanationHtml: Arjuna calls the form now before him gentle and human. On seeing it, he regains his composure and returns to his normal state. This follows the request for the four-armed appearance in 11.46 and Sanjaya's report that Krishna has shown his own gentle form. Arjuna's reply states the relief that the change of form brings him.

verses.meaningHtml: The blessed Lord said: This form of mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold. Even the gods continually long for a sight of this form.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna says that the form Arjuna has seen is very difficult to behold and that even the gods continually desire its sight. The words follow the return to a gentle human appearance after the universal vision. “This form” is thus spoken within that sequence. Krishna then explains which practices cannot secure such a sight and names undivided devotion as its means.

verses.meaningHtml: Neither through the Vedas, nor through austerity, gifts or sacrifice, can I be seen in this way as you have seen me.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna repeats that the Vedas, austerities, gifts and sacrifice do not enable a person to see him as Arjuna has seen him. The same practices were excluded as means in 11.48. Here the exclusion leads immediately to the declaration that undivided devotion enables true knowledge, sight and entry into him.

verses.meaningHtml: But through undivided devotion, Arjuna, I can in this way be known, seen in truth and entered, scorcher of foes.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna states that undivided devotion enables him to be known, seen in truth and entered. Ananyā bhakti means devotion directed to him without another object. The three acts of knowing, seeing and entering are all included in the promise. This follows the exclusion of Vedic learning, austerity, gifts and sacrifice as means of obtaining the sight Arjuna has received.

verses.meaningHtml: One who acts for me, holds me as the highest end, is devoted to me, is free from attachment and bears hostility toward no being—that person comes to me, Pandava.
verses.explanationHtml: Krishna names five conditions of the person who comes to him: acting for him, taking him as the highest goal, being his devotee, abandoning attachment and bearing hostility toward no being. Action, purpose, devotion and disposition are all specified. The promise of coming to Krishna is attached to this combination of service to him, exclusive aim, non-attachment and absence of enmity.
